passage:
"It was nothing, the ref is blind!" Marek's voice cracked over the canteen noise in Gdańsk. Santiago slid his phone across the table. The replay showed the striker Marek worshipped stamping on a defender's ankle after the whistle.
"Everyone does that," Marek said, jaw tight, and pushed his tray away. All afternoon he typed angry replies under a critic's post.
That night he watched the replay again, alone and slowly. The stamp was clear. His stomach dropped, not because he liked the player less, but because he had shouted "nothing" so loudly.
Next morning he told Santiago, "Okay. It was a foul. I can still like him and say that."
Santiago nodded. "That's all I wanted."

qa.q: What did the replay show the striker doing?
qa.a: It showed the striker stamping on a defender's ankle after the whistle.

qa.q: Why did Marek's stomach drop when he watched the replay alone?
qa.a: He saw that the foul was real and remembered shouting "nothing" so loudly; he felt uneasy about his fierce defence, not because he liked the player less.

qa.q: What could Marek do next time his idol is criticised?
qa.a: He could listen to the criticism, look at the evidence, and admit what is fair while still liking the player, so loyalty doesn't switch off his own judgment.

qa.q: How might Santiago have seen Marek's outburst in the canteen?
qa.a: Santiago probably saw a friend too heated to look at the replay, and wanted honesty from him rather than for him to stop liking the player.

grounding: Shows a teen defending an idol against fair criticism, then reclaiming his own judgment.

passage:
"Did you see what they're saying about Veer Rathore?" Mridul asked, holding out his phone.

Pranav didn't even look. "Whatever it is, it's lies. Jealous people."

"It's a video. He was driving his car at, like, a crazy speed on a highway with no seatbelt, filming himself."

"So? He's the best batter in the country."

"Both can be true, Pranav."

"You just hate him." Pranav's voice was rising.

"I don't hate him. I have his poster too. But if my cousin did that, you'd say he was an idiot."

Pranav opened his mouth. Then he actually watched the video. Veer, laughing, the speedometer climbing, no hands on the wheel for a second.

He went quiet. "That's… really dangerous."

"Yeah."

"He's still an amazing player."

"He is. And he did a dumb, dangerous thing." Mridul pocketed the phone. "You can say both. I do."

qa.q: What was Veer Rathore doing in the video?
qa.a: He was driving his car at a crazy speed on a highway with no seatbelt, filming himself.

qa.q: Why did Pranav defend Veer before even looking?
qa.a: Pranav felt fiercely loyal and protective of his idol, and felt attacked when anyone criticised him.

qa.q: What helped Pranav use his own judgment?
qa.a: Mridul asked what Pranav would say if a cousin did the same, and then Pranav actually watched the video instead of dismissing it.

qa.q: How does Mridul see Veer Rathore?
qa.a: Mridul admires Veer's playing but thinks his driving was dangerous, holding both views at once.

grounding: It shows a teen who fiercely defends his idol even against fair criticism, and learns that loyalty should not switch off his own judgment.

passage:
In Class 11, I would have fought anyone who said a word against my favourite singer. I'm Rafiq, and I had every song on repeat.

Then at a concert, which I watched on a livestream, he mocked a girl in the front row for crying. Called her "drama queen" into the mic. Everyone laughed. A clip of it went everywhere.

People online called him cruel. I jumped in, commenting all night: she was faking, he was joking, haters. My friend Harish messaged, "Rafiq, you'd never say that if it was your sister in the crowd."

That stopped me. Because it was true. If anyone had done that to my Apa, I'd have been furious.

I looked at the clip again, properly this time. The girl's face after he said it. She wasn't faking anything.

I deleted my comments. I still love a lot of his songs. But I stopped defending him for everything. Loving someone's music doesn't mean I have to switch my brain off.

qa.q: What did the singer call the girl in the front row?
qa.a: He called her "drama queen" into the mic.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling after Harish's message?
qa.a: Rafiq felt uncomfortable and ashamed, realising how angry Rafiq would feel if it were Rafiq's own sister.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that showed Rafiq's own judgment returning?
qa.a: Rafiq watched the clip again properly, deleted the comments and stopped defending the singer for everything.

qa.q: How might the girl in the front row feel about the singer's words?
qa.a: She probably felt humiliated and hurt, especially as the clip spread everywhere.

grounding: It shows a teen who defends an idol fiercely even when the criticism is fair, and learns that loyalty should not switch off their own judgment.
